claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure with multilevel chemical fluctuations and phase boundaries.
A physics-informed, multi-fidelity machine-learning framework using microstructural descriptors can predict tensile and fracture properties of HfNbTiVAl10.
The proposed framework will overcome the computational inefficiency of prior approaches.
The proposed framework will improve prediction accuracy for Young’s modulus, yield strength, and toughness.
Local composition variance and phase-distribution parameters can quantitatively represent the hierarchical chemical fluctuations.
Hierarchical chemical-fluctuation descriptors mediate the relationship between microstructural heterogeneity and macroscopic mechanical response.
The model will be trained using approximately 100 high-fidelity DFT/CALPHAD data points.
Synthetic data will be used to augment the high-fidelity training set and represent microstructural complexity.
The model will be calibrated using targeted tensile and fracture experiments at ambient and moderately elevated temperatures.
Embedding physical constraints and microstructural descriptors reduces the effective prediction space.
Synthetic-data augmentation ensures that the model captures essential microstructural effects.
Targeted experimental calibration improves model interpretability and accuracy.
The method is expected to reduce computational cost by more than a factor of ten.
The method is expected to attain R2 greater than 0.98 for Young’s modulus.
The method is expected to attain R2 greater than 0.98 for yield strength.
The method is expected to reduce the mean absolute error of toughness predictions by approximately 40% relative to full-scale simulations.
Exhaustive DFT/CALPHAD, full-scale finite-element, and Monte Carlo phase-field approaches are computationally demanding and struggle to predict toughness precisely.
The approach may become unreliable when synthetic data do not capture the full heterostructural complexity.
The approach may become unreliable at very high strain rates or temperatures where new deformation mechanisms emerge.
Prediction errors exceeding approximately 20% for any measured property in blinded tests will falsify the hypothesis.
